Upgrade Ableton Live or make a DAW?

I am reconsidering my earlier decision to keep Ableton Live and avoid the distraction of replacing it with something custom. I currently use Ableton/Live 11. A sale on the Live 12 upgrade, which would include Live 13, runs through the end of the year; I understand the discount is about 20%.
Upgrade Ableton Live or make a DAW?

Live 12 would make some of my work easier: it has a newer JavaScript engine, and some Model Context Protocol integrations require Live 12 or later. I am lukewarm on the browser improvements. Live 13's keyboard-friendly device tray, with easier access to devices and copying between tracks, sounds compelling, but I am not desperate for the new features.
Upgrade Ableton Live or make a DAW?

AI integration is the larger question. As I understand it, Live 13 has no official MCP, command-line tool, or API for the kind of integration I want. If Ableton does not provide one, I am unsure whether I want to keep using Live. An upgrade could add fuel to my creative life for a while, but it would not settle that question.
Upgrade Ableton Live or make a DAW?

My/Pref/Aesthetic/DIY makes me want to get closer to a problem by making something that just fits my needs. That preference has limits. I use LazyVim rather than build my own Neovim distribution because a shared tool benefits from many people's attention, while my own attention is limited.

I also know my pattern: I gain creative momentum, then start an ambitious technical project. The technical project absorbs the time I meant to spend making music, and eventually I have to stop. Building a digital audio workstation could repeat that pattern.

Live also gives me a shared language. At yesterday's synth meetup, I could explain my set layout to other musicians who knew Ableton. A DAW of my own might feel like paddling away from that community; I would have to explain both the setup and why I made it.

A cello is a particular shape that has been co-evolved over time to meet the needs of humans. If a practiced cellist sits with any other person's cello, they can play an f# because of certain shared creative constraints.
A DAW that can grow with me

My experience with Logseq Gardener makes the alternative attractive. With AI agents, I have gradually built a faster, more customizable Rust-based static site generator around files I can commit to Git. The Person/codekiln/GitHub/gitpa Ghost in the Patch Alpha site has a custom player, illuminations, and pages that explain or illustrate Ableton sets. I can keep shaping the tools as I discover what I want, and that control feels like a tailwind for creation.
A DAW that can grow with me

The work took months and is still in progress; I have just started on a language server and want to interact with Logseq through Neovim. Starting a DAW later would also postpone the long period in which it could grow with me gradually.
A DAW that can grow with me

As time goes on, AI/Capability/Exponential Growth of starts to create a vast AI/Capability/Overhang I it will become more and more important to be more ambitious with the utilization of AI. A solution scoped too narrowly today might become inflexible as newer models make larger projects possible. Building software with AI also shows how I construct things with AI, and can become part of my portfolio.
A DAW that can grow with me

My DAW might take inspiration from Live but reflect different priorities: version control, hackability, clean APIs, and integration with other open, hackable tools. I am interested in a text-file-based DAW integrated with Logseq, a contemporary alternative to Csound.
A DAW that can grow with me

I want a self-hosted system that lets me work without tracking which hard drive contains each asset, and a seamless experience across desktop and phone so I can edit outside. A private cloud is a possibility, though I would need to decide where to draw the line on infrastructure.
A DAW that can grow with me

I could offer the software for free and explore an AGPL license or a Linux-first design. If hosting were involved, I would only need enough paying users to cover hosting or hardware costs. The design problem itself appeals to me: why pay someone else to carry the burden of a problem I am interested in solving?
A DAW that can grow with me

I practiced Piano for an upcoming event today for the first time in a long time. It was like coming home. There's something so special about the state of attention that comes from inventing practice techniques for 3+ hours. Sitting with the piano, there's nothing else. Everything else dissolves. It's a deeper channel of music for me. That part of my brain goes way back.

The connection to making sounds with synths and organs goes way back for me, too; some of my earliest memories are playing organ and synth as well as piano. Organ and synth has always let me explore the space of timbre. Piano lets me explore the space of structure and articulation.

I'm nervous that playing piano will take me away from my newly rediscovered practice of synth. It feels comparatively more nascent and in need of nurturing. The event is in just under two weeks. If I go for that long without making any synth music, it could knock my balance off.

Part of the problem is that I have more experience with the phases of piano practice. There's warmups, technique practice, sight reading practice, slow detail practice, memorization practice, performance practice. Most of these are piano-bound, though a few, like listening to performances, is not.

With synth, these forms aren't as well developed, at least, they aren't as mature in my practice. There's configuring Ableton/Live/Sets, there's tweaking Launchpad/Custom modes, there's exploration of how sounds work in Microfreak/Presets, there's trying to get to know a workflow that uses the Launchpad/Sequencer more intuitively, there's asking and researching questions about my equipment, there's capturing samples, processing samples, there's writing software to facilitate various parts of the musical process. So many parts of these are screen-bound and provide me with many opportunities for distraction. If the piano is good at distracting me, it's because I want to make more different kinds of music with it. The synth's relationship to the computer is the opposite. The ways in which it's good at distracting me lead me farther from making music.

I think I might need a more organized sense of when to do instrument building vs when to do music improv vs when to do set building. I'm into the style of "composition" that inolves constructing the instrument for improvisation and a structure for the performance. That involves all of these styles of "practice," and more.

One thing that has been confusing me a bit lately is whether to continue using the four colors of the Launchpad/Sequencer to structure my Ableton/Live/Sets. I think I might want to make some Launchpad/Custom modes that send sysex messages to set a specific preset to be one that I know. I might also want to make a few custom modes broken into quadrants for certain colors, when have each quadrant represent pads, sfx, etc. I've also been thinking about making a few innstruments that use the built-in devices in Ableton, maybe a few drum racks I've customized.
A man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack is when an attacker secretly positions themselves between two parties and intercepts their communication.
Conceptually, it breaks trust in the channel rather than necessarily breaking the app itself.
Common outcomes include eavesdropping, message tampering, credential theft, or session hijacking when integrity and authenticity checks are weak or absent.

Can I browse man pages by heading, including in nvim or LazyVim?

Short answer: man finds and formats a manual page, then hands the result to a pager. The macOS man program and its usual pager, less, do not expose the page's headings as a navigable hierarchy. Neovim's built-in man-page viewer does: open the page with :Man tmux, then press gO for a table of contents.
Can I browse man pages by heading, including in nvim or LazyVim?
Can I browse man pages by heading, including in nvim or LazyVim?

The installed /usr/bin/man accepts -P pager; MANPAGER overrides PAGER. Its default is less, whose navigation is text-based: search for an uppercase heading with /^COMMANDS$, then use n and N to move among matches. A broader search such as /^[A-Z][A-Z0-9 /_-]*$ finds many top-level headings. less does not parse those matches into an outline. Answer/Official from OpenBSD man(1) and less(1).
Can I browse man pages by heading, including in nvim or LazyVim?

This machine currently sets MANPAGER to col -bx | bat --language=man --style=plain --paging=always. CLI/Tool/bat supplies highlighting and invokes a pager for scrolling, but it does not add heading-aware navigation.

In the man-page buffer, gO opens a location-list outline. Select an entry and press Enter to jump to it; q closes the outline or man window. On the installed tmux(1) page, Neovim finds the main headings plus many indented command and option entries, so the outline is more detailed than a list of top-level sections.
Can I browse man pages by heading, including in nvim or LazyVim?
Put the cursor on a reference such as printf(3) and press K or Ctrl-] to open that man page; Ctrl-T returns. Answer/Official from Neovim's man-page documentation and gO outline documentation.
Can I browse man pages by heading, including in nvim or LazyVim?

For a one-off shell invocation using Neovim as the pager: MANPAGER='nvim +Man!' MANWIDTH=999 man tmux. MANWIDTH=999 reduces hard wrapping before Neovim receives the formatted page. To make this the default, export those variables in the shell configuration; that would replace the current bat-based MANPAGER pipeline.

Can I browse man pages by heading, including in nvim or LazyVim?

The current LazyVim setup uses the nvim/Plugin/snacks.nvim/Picker. <leader>sM opens its Man Pages picker, which searches for a page to open. After choosing tmux(1), press gO in the resulting man buffer to browse its internal outline. The picker chooses a manual page; Neovim's built-in gO provides the heading navigation. Answer/Official from LazyVim's Snacks picker mappings.

Best fit: use :Man tmux followed by gO when hierarchy matters. Keep man tmux with the current bat pager for quick linear reading and text search.
